title: Liberals won't pull advance requests out of MAID legislation for separate vote: minister

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Liberal government will not pull advance directives out of its update to medically assisted dying legislation so MPs can vote on the measure separately, Justice Minister Sean Fraser told a committee of MPs on Thursday.
Justice minister says just because there's no deadline for advance requests doesn't mean issue isn't urgent

The Liberal government will not pull advance directives out of its bill updating medically assisted dying legislation so MPs can vote on the measure separately, Justice Minister Sean Fraser told a committee of MPs on Thursday.
"I think we have an opportunity to minimize suffering, which is every bit as important or more than meeting legislative timelines," Fraser said.

Conservative MPs on the justice committee pressed the minister to explain why Bill C-41, his legislation updating medical assistance in dying (MAID) legislation, is being pushed through Parliament without allowing MPs to vote on its two principle amendments separately. It was introduced in the House of Commons on Oct. 27.
One amendment bans people from receiving a medically assisted death if they only have a mental illness, while the other allows people with diminishing mental capacity to request MAID in advance.

"Why are you not splitting the bill, why are you forcing parliamentarians to proceed with what you acknowledge is a complex issue on a timeline that doesn't need to be in place for advance requests," Conservative MP Andrew Lawton asked Fraser.
Feds won't split advance directives out of MAID legislation: justice minister
The government passed MAID legislation in 2016. But the Superior Court of Quebec struck the law down in 2019 because it was limited to those whose deaths were "reasonably foreseeable."

Bill C-7, which was passed in Parliament in March 2021, removed that requirement, in line with the court's ruling, while temporarily pushing back the expansion of MAID to cases involving only mental illness to March 2023.

The mental health provision was then further delayed to 2024 and again to March 2027, which means that unless Bill C-41 is passed or the government pushes back the date again, MAID will automatically expand to cover mental illness in March of next year.
It's about preventing suffering, Fraser says

The amendment that allows people to give advance consent when the illness they're suffering from will eventually eliminate their ability to make that decision is not impacted by a legislative timeline.

"Though there is a legislated timeline in place on the mental illness issue, I don't want to suggest that the advance request issue is not also urgent," Fraser said in explaining his decision not to split the bill.

The minister told MPs that the decision to keep both amendments in the same bill was not based on medical advice but on his concern that delaying advance requests further would lead to unnecessary suffering.

blocks.text: "My motivation to move forward expeditiously with that issue is borne out by conversations I've had with people who are suffering," Fraser said.

"It's a very painful thing to sit down with someone who knows that their life is about to come to an end, that has the added challenge of being on the verge of losing their capacity to make decisions for themselves."
Proper safeguards in place
Fraser said the issue has been studied and that as long as the proper safeguards are in place to ensure advance requests are properly managed, the legislation should proceed swiftly.
The minister said Bill C-41 is safe because a doctor who is an expert in the illness someone is afflicted with must sign off on the conditions for when MAID can be administered.

Fraser said that two separate medical assessors then must work independently to determine when the conditions signed off by the expert doctor have been met while also being satisfied that the person's suffering is intolerable and the illness is incurable.
"That's when the person would be rendered eligible for medical assistance in dying under the proposed approach," he said.
Fraser said people who may no longer recognize themselves or others but who appear happy and enjoying life would not be eligible because they are not experiencing intolerable suffering.
